/-!
# Erdős Problem 1094

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/1094](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1094)
-/

namespace Erdos1094

open scoped Nat

/--
For all $n\ge 2k$ the least prime factor of $\binom{n}{k}$ is $\le\max(n/k,k)$, with only
finitely many exceptions.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_1094 :
    {(n, k) : ℕ × ℕ | 0 < k ∧ 2 * k ≤ n ∧ (n.choose k).minFac > max (n / k) k}.Finite := by
  sorry

end Erdos1094

reformulations.difference: The Lean exceptional-pair predicate uses natural-number division in max (n / k) k, whereas the source's n/k is an ordinary real or rational quotient.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For k > 0 and an integer p, floor(n/k) < p iff n < p*k iff (n : ℝ)/k < p. Combining this with k < p proves max (n / k) k < p iff max ((n : ℝ)/k) (k : ℝ) < (p : ℝ). Thus the natural-division and real-division exceptional sets are exactly equal, so their finiteness assertions are equivalent. This was proved in /workspace/review/equivalence.lean, along with equivalence to a uniform bound holding for all sufficiently large n and every admissible k; the proofs do not depend on sorryAx.

review.notes: Checked the sole declaration against the source's main finiteness conjecture; the stronger conjecture specifying exactly 14 exceptions is not asserted by this file. The source still records OPEN. Lean proofs establish that 0 < k and 2*k ≤ n imply 1 < n.choose k, excluding minFac's exceptional inputs 0 and 1, and verify the bounds for k = 1 and n = 2*k. Exhaustive evaluation for n ≤ 300 finds exactly the source's 14 listed exceptional pairs, as a sanity check only. Both scratch files compile successfully.
